title: Every heart a jewel
hookLine: don't speak one harsh word; the Master is in all; don't break any heart, every heart is a jewel (Farid salok, ang 1384)

cards: A jeweler's counter. The stones sit on black velvet, and nobody handles them roughly. Even the person who sweeps the shop at night is careful near that glass.
Something that precious changes how everyone moves around it, and how they speak near it, too.
Farid takes that picture and sets it somewhere unexpected: inside every person you'll talk to today, including the ones who annoy you.

teach.b: The couplets are on Ang 1384, near the end of Farid's saloks. The first, in paraphrase: don't speak even one harsh word; the True Master lives in everyone. Don't break anyone's heart; all of them are priceless jewels.
We heard that line once in year one. Today, two things in it. First, the word for harsh.

Farid's word is phika: flat, tasteless, without sweetness, like food with no salt. So the harsh word isn't only a shout. It's the cold, flat word too: the curt reply, the sigh, the answer with nothing kind in it.
Two days ago Farid's bread was plain and enough. A plain word is fine. A word with the sweetness drained out on purpose is what he warns against.
Second, the reason. He doesn't say be nice because it's polite.

teach.h: THE TRUE MASTER IS IN EVERYONE.
teach.b: He says the True Master is in everyone. Speak flatly to a person and you're speaking that way to the place where the Lord lives.
The next couplet pushes further, in paraphrase: every mind is a jewel, and breaking one is not good at all.

teach.h: LONG FOR THE BELOVED; BREAK NO HEART.
teach.b: If you long for your Beloved, don't break anyone's heart.
That's the turn. For Farid, love of God and care for people aren't two projects. The longing for the Beloved is exactly what forbids the harsh word.
You can't want the jeweler and smash the jewels. Sikhs hear this beside the Gurus' own teaching that one light is in all, and they sing Farid's couplet in that light.

how: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read this couplet together with the Gurus' teaching that the one light of God is in all people.

o: a flat, harsh word, with the sweetness drained out
a sweet word offered to win someone over
a jewel too precious to be handled roughly

games.q: inside the couplets — tap the pairs.
p: why no heart should be broken

s: Farid's harsh word means only shouting
his word is phika: flat, tasteless, the cold word with no sweetness in it.
his reason is that the True Master lives in everyone.
Farid ties longing for the Beloved to not breaking hearts
if you long for your Beloved, he says, don't break anyone's heart.

games.q: you love God and long for the Beloved. someone in front of you is being difficult, and a flat, cold answer is ready. what does Farid say?
o: the longing is for God; people are a separate matter.
if you long for the Beloved, don't break anyone's heart.
games.why: for Farid, love of God and care for people are one longing: every heart is a jewel, and the Master lives in it.

practice: Think through who you'll speak with before tonight, and pause on the one you're most likely to be flat with; picture the jewel on black velvet, there, inside them.
Then say one ordinary sentence to them silently, twice, once flat and once with a little sweetness left in it, and hear the difference. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Phika. Farid's word for the harsh, flat word without sweetness: don't speak it, because the True Master lives in everyone and every heart is a priceless jewel.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a jewel, a ruby; Farid's word for every heart.

carryVoice: Your line: add one grain of sweetness. A plain word can still be a kind one. That's day seven hundred sixty-six.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid (ik phika na gaalaae; sabhna man maanik), Ang 1384
